newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire prime minister under fire over war in east.
newsitem.headline: Zaire prime minister under fire over war in east.

text.p: Zaire's part-Tutsi prime minister, Kengo wa Dondo, architect of Western-backed economic reforms in his corruption-plagued nation, is in the firing line as Tutsi rebels advance in the east.

On Saturday, the usually reticent army chief of staff General Eluki Monga said publicly that Kengo and his government had been too slow in providing the means to fight against the rebels and soldiers from Tutsi-led Rwanda.
"We regret that the government is moving too slowly and has not yet given us the necessary means," he told a Kinshasa news conference, appealing for more weapons.

On Friday, protesters marched on Kengo's office calling for his removal and representatives of his bitter rival Etienne Tshisekedi in neighbouring Congo have gone so far as to call on the army to arrest him for high treason.
Kengo, who has shown himself to be an astute political player in the past, has opted for a business as usual approach.

"When a war starts people look for a scapegoat," he told reporters after Friday's protests. "Today it happens to be the prime minister and his government, but I will continue to work without listening to malicious gossip."
The army's public criticism is potentially more serious but once again the Kengo camp sought to play down the outburst.

"The government will not react to the army accusations. It is not a time for division," Information Minister Boguo Makeli told Reuters, adding that the government had done what it could and would try to find more cash.

But political pundits say that the entry of the army into the political fray could well herald the beginning of the end for Kengo, who was voted into office as a compromise candidate by Zaire's transitional assembly in 1994.
"This time it looks serious. The fact that it is the army that's saying this could well be used as a justification to remove the prime minister," one said.
"We still don't know where Mobutu stands," he added.

Veteran strongman Mobutu Sese Seko, who seized power in 1965 and ruled virtually unchallenged until 1990 when foreign and domestic pressure forced him to embrace democratic reform, has been out of the country since August, when he had surgery for prostate cancer in Switzerland.

Kengo's attempts to reform Zaire's economy, while resented by many of Mobutu's placemen who found themselves targeted, helped raise the president's flagging profile in the West -- where he was accused of human rights abuses and corruption and treated as a virtual pariah.

In the past, Kengo has neutralised any challenge with the support of the veteran strongman, who arguably remains Zaire's sole symbol of national unity and whose supporters enjoy a majority in the transitional assembly.
Zaire went through seven prime ministers between the beginning of democratic reforms and Kengo's election. Kengo has lasted far longer than any of the others.

But this time the attacks are compounded by a wave of anti-Rwandan and particularly anti-Tutsi feeling -- which has seen Tutsi-owned shops in the capital attacked and has triggered a mini exodus of Tutsis who figured prominently in Kinshasa's business and professional classes.
Kengo's mother was part Tutsi, his father was Polish.
The transitional parliament summoned Kengo to explain his conduct of the war publicly -- and then recommended that anyone of Tutsi origin be made to leave jobs in public service.
Political analysts say that certain generals resent Kengo's economic reforms, which aim to minimise corruption and restore macroeconomic stability after years of hyperinflation.

"The sheer fact of the war is itself going to make continuing reforms difficult with calls for greater spending," one Western diplomat said. "If the generals push Kengo to start printing more money then the gains of the past two years will be lost."
But overhanging everything is Mobutu's illness and his own haunting own prophecy that without "the guide" -- as he likes to be known -- the sprawling Central African state will collapse.
The armed forces are divided into units with varying degrees of training, equipment and pay, and with only Mobutu as a common commander in chief.
"If the president had been here the government would not have moved slowly to provide for the war," said Eluki.
"The truth is nobody here really knows the state of the president's health and that may make it hard for any army officer to take over on his own behalf," said one Western diplomat.
"If someone tried by himself and did not succeed there could be very serious trouble," he added.
